data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The night-time UHI gap is primarily controlled by urban geometry\u2014specifically the sky view factor\u2014where deep street canyons trap longwave radiation, and the gap scales inversely with the sky view factor and proportional to building height.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If a city consists entirely of single-story buildings with an unobstructed sky view, the radiation trapping effect is nullified.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If overcast clouds dominate both urban and rural skies, longwave cooling is uniformly suppressed everywhere, erasing the sky view factor differential.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"On clear nights, surfaces cool by emitting longwave radiation to the cold sky. In dense cities, tall buildings reduce the sky view factor, creating a horizon that intercepts and re-radiates emitted longwave radiation back to the surface. This radiation trapping slows the urban cooling rate significantly compared to the open countryside. Cross-city variance is explained by urban morphology: cities with taller buildings, deeper street canyons, and denser built structures have a lower sky view factor, leading to a more pronounced night-time UHI.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
